analysis.one_liner: Gives car owners and independent repair shops access to vehicle data and repair tools.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 45 cosponsors that would force automakers to share repair data and tools with independent shops cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote in February 2026 but has never reached a full committee or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The REPAIR Act would bar car manufacturers from using technological or contractual barriers to keep owners and independent repair shops from getting a vehicle's diagnostic data, repair instructions, and tools. Automakers would have to share that information on the same terms, at the same cost, and at the same time they give it to their own dealers. It also cancels contract clauses where buyers waive these rights, sets data-privacy rules for shops that access the data, and lets the Federal Trade Commission take complaints and enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners, who could get their vehicles fixed at any shop of their choosing instead of paying dealer service prices; independent repair shops, which gain access to the same data and tools dealers use; and aftermarket parts and diagnostic-tool makers, who can sell compatible products. Owners also gain privacy protections: shops must delete data on request within 72 hours and cannot sell it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to give owners, independent shops, and aftermarket parts and tool makers access to vehicle-generated data and critical repair information on the same terms, at the same time and cost, that dealers and authorized service providers get.
Bars manufacturers from using technological barriers, contract waivers, or requirements to use a particular brand of parts or tools to force owners back to dealer service departments.

Gives owners control over their own car data: they can revoke a repair shop's access at any time, have their data deleted within 72 hours of asking, and shops cannot sell or resell the data without consent.

Creates an FTC complaint process so any person can file a complaint about a violation, with the FTC required to investigate and conclude within five months, and treats violations as unfair or deceptive practices under FTC law.

Sets up a federal advisory committee, with seats for independent repair shops, consumer organizations, insurers, and trucking companies alongside automakers and dealers, to report on barriers to competitive repair.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers and franchised car dealers. Manufacturers would bear the cost of opening up data interfaces and publishing repair information, and they and their dealers would give up some of the service and parts revenue they earn when owners have no choice but to come to them for diagnostics and repairs.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state law: once enacted, states could not keep or enforce their own rules on vehicle repair data access, so a state that passed a stronger law (Massachusetts has one) would see it overridden by this federal floor.

Manufacturers are still allowed to keep cryptographic and technological protections they deem necessary to secure data and safety systems, so in practice the promised access could still be limited by the same companies it restricts.
Vehicles equipped with automated driving systems (self-driving vehicles) are excluded from the bill's data-access requirements entirely, leaving a growing slice of the fleet out.
Enforcement runs only through FTC complaints and agency action; there is no private right to sue a manufacturer directly, so an owner blocked from repair data depends entirely on FTC follow-through.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For car owners and independent shops the upside is concrete: cheaper repair options and the right to fix a car you own without the manufacturer's permission. The real costs fall on automakers and dealers as compliance expense and lost service revenue, some of which could be passed into vehicle prices. The main trade-off a supporter has to acknowledge is the preemption of state laws, which trades possibly stronger state protections for one national standard, and the bill's own carve-outs (cryptographic protections, self-driving vehicles) leave manufacturers room to keep some barriers in place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill passed its subcommittee by voice vote in February 2026 and is now sitting at the full House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not scheduled a vote on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Neal Dunn introduced the bill on February 25, 2025, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade.
The bill drew 45 cosponsors, split almost evenly between 23 Democrats and 22 Republicans, making it one of the more bipartisan repair bills in Congress.
On February 10, 2026, the subcommittee held a markup session and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote, but the full committee has taken no action since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and franchised dealers are better off for now: they keep control of repair data and dealer service revenue while the bill waits for a full committee vote that has not been scheduled.

for.name: Rep. Neal P. Dunn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the REPAIR Act and recruited a bipartisan group of 16 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 45 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors across party lines, giving the bill bipartisan support in the House.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade
for.role: House subcommittee with jurisdiction over the bill
for.what_they_did: Held a consideration and mark-up session on February 10, 2026, and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and members controlling the committee's calendar
against.what_they_did: Have not scheduled a full committee markup or vote in the year since the subcommittee forwarded the bill, leaving it stalled at the committee stage.

against.name: Auto manufacturers (Alliance for Automotive Innovation)
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed federal right-to-repair mandates of this kind, arguing they create security and safety risks and intrude on proprietary systems.

against.name: Franchised dealership groups
against.what_they_did: Have opposed right-to-repair legislation that would route repair work and data away from dealer service departments.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support is genuinely bipartisan: of its 45 cosponsors, 23 are Democrats and 22 are Republicans, and it cleared subcommittee on a voice vote rather than a party-line roll call.

industries.note: The bill bars automakers from locking owners and shops out of vehicle data and repair tools and voids contract clauses that waive those rights, cutting into their control of the repair process. They would carry the compliance cost of open data access.

Dealer service departments currently profit when owners must come to them for diagnostics and warranty-adjacent repairs. Equal access for independent shops means competing for that business, though dealers gain one of eleven seats on the bill's advisory committee.

Shops would get the same diagnostic data, repair procedures, and tools as dealers, letting them compete for repairs they are now locked out of. Owner-designation rules also protect shops' continued access when a customer chooses them.

industries.industry: Aftermarket parts and diagnostic tool makers
industries.note: Manufacturers could no longer block compatible aftermarket parts or require branded tools, opening a market that makers of independent parts, remanufactured parts, and diagnostic equipment are currently restricted from serving.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared subcommittee and now needs a full Energy and Commerce Committee markup and vote before it could reach the House floor. The previous Congress's version of the REPAIR Act also gathered bipartisan cosponsors and never got past committee, and with no full-committee action more than a year after introduction, the most likely path is that it stays parked in committee unless supporters force the issue through leadership.
